seo.title: Elasticsearch client for {devices}
seo.description: Send Query DSL from a console, browse Elasticsearch indices as tables, filter, sort and edit documents by _id, signed in with a password or API key.

header.title: Elasticsearch client for {devices}
header.lead: A console for Query DSL requests, and a grid that reads each index as a table and edits documents by their _id. Neither runs on SQL: every action is a REST request to the cluster.

sections.title: Connect
paragraphs: Enter the cluster’s host and REST port and pick an Auth Method. Username & Password sends HTTP Basic. API Key sends the field in an Authorization: ApiKey header, so paste the encoded value a create API key request returns. None suits a development cluster with security off. A connection reaches one cluster, so the form has no Database field.

New connections start with SSL Disabled, which is plain HTTP. Every other mode uses HTTPS: Preferred and Required (skip verify) accept a self-signed certificate, and Verify CA and Verify Identity check it. Elasticsearch 8.x turns security and TLS on by default, so an 8.x cluster usually needs HTTPS and credentials.

sections.title: Indices and the Query DSL console
paragraphs: The console takes a method, a path and an optional JSON body, the way Kibana Dev Tools does, such as GET /orders/_search with a match query. Search hits come back as rows, _cat requests with format=json and other array responses become a table, and anything else shows as formatted JSON. The _sql endpoint is not reachable.

The sidebar lists indices as tables and hides names that begin with a dot. Columns come from the mapping: object fields flatten to dotted paths such as address.city, a nested field gets one JSON column for its array plus a column per leaf, and every document carries _id, _index and _score.

Column filters become term, range, wildcard, terms and exists queries, and the Raw SQL filter row takes Lucene syntax, such as name:Widget, sent as a query_string. Sorting a text field uses its .keyword subfield when the mapping has one.

Grid edits become REST calls keyed by _id: _update for a changed document, _doc to create or delete one. Type an _id into a new row to name the document. Change a nested array through its JSON column; a value typed into one of its leaf columns stops the save, which names the column and sends nothing.

sections.title: Mappings
paragraphs: Mappings are read-only in TablePro. Truncate is not offered, because the nearest thing Elasticsearch has, _delete_by_query, runs asynchronously and reports conflicts per document; send it from the console. Deleting an index from the sidebar sends the DELETE request its confirmation shows.

sections.title: Export
paragraphs: There is no import. Export reads a whole index with a point-in-time and search_after, so it is not capped at the result window, and writes CSV, JSON or XLSX.

faq.question: Can I page past the result window?
faq.answer: Yes. Paging past Elasticsearch’s default window switches to search_after over a point-in-time. The switch happens at the default, so an index with a lowered max_result_window errors before it; raise the setting back to the default.

faq.question: Why does sorting by _id leave the rows in the same order?
faq.answer: Elasticsearch cannot sort on _id, or on a text field with no .keyword subfield, so TablePro drops that column from the sort. Add a keyword subfield to the mapping, or sort on a keyword field.
